E0001.summary: A scriptural passage (cap. 3, v. 7) Atwood cites in support of the point that it is God who gives the increase.
E0001.body: Cited by Atwood, with the reference cap. 3, v. 7 given in the footnote, in support of the point that the increase comes from God: “neither he that watereth, but God, that giveth the increase” [IV.1 ¶40; IV.1 n32].

E0003.summary: An abbot Atwood cites as having praised the Hermetic Art and the wisdom of Arnold.
E0003.body: Cited by Atwood as one who praised the Hermetic Art and Arnold's wisdom [I.1 ¶43].

E0004.summary: Named as the addressee of Aquinas' Thesaurus Alchimiae.
E0004.body: Mentioned only as the person to whom Aquinas' *Thesaurus Alchimiae* is addressed [I.1 ¶42; I.1 n49; I.1 n51].

E0005.summary: In a view attributed to Plato, the defective reasoning by negation through which Matter is apprehended, describing it only by what it is not.
E0005.body: A quoted view (Plato): Matter can be apprehended, but only by a reasoning that proceeds by negation, describing it by what it is not: “Matter is indeed to be apprehended, and that by a sort of defective or ablative reasoning” [III.2 ¶53].

E0006.summary: Cited through the Sepher Jezirah (Liber de Creatione) as an example of the wisely simple, and elsewhere for travelling with his asses.
E0006.body: Atwood cites the *Sepher Jezirah* (*Liber de Creatione, Authore Abraham*, cap. 1), presenting Abraham as an example of the wisely simple who subdued the will to the Law of Wisdom, and closing with a Latin injunction: “Intellige in scientia et sepias intellignetia” [II.3 ¶55; II.3 n61; II.3 ¶56; II.3 n62] (our rendering, roughly: understand in knowledge and be wise in understanding). Elsewhere he is mentioned, by way of illustration, as one who constantly travelled with his asses [III.2 ¶64].

E0007.summary: Mentioned as the one who indicated the fire and the furnace to Flamel.
E0007.body: Mentioned by Atwood as the one who indicated the fire and furnace to Flamel [III.1 ¶37].

E0009.summary: The ultimate foundation of knowledge; philosophers dispute its conditions and difficulty, but, Atwood says, none deny that it is possible.
E0009.body: Atwood's term for the ultimate ground of knowledge. She notes that “philosophers have disputed about the conditions and difficulty of the Absolute ground” [II.1 ¶33]; the record adds that none deny its possibility.

E0010.summary: What the hypostasis bounding abstract reason proves to be when met by the inquiring light within; prior to all duality of consciousness.
E0010.body: In Atwood's account, the hypostasis that bounds abstract reason, when met by the inquiring light within, proves to be Absolute Identity, “which, before all duality of consciousness, is the fortitude and life of all” [III.2 ¶31]. She also speaks of the “incomprehensible nature of the objective contact in Identity” [III.2 ¶33].

E0011.summary: In a quoted account, the abyss where the parts of the world lay mingled and formless before the spirit's breath agitated the mass.
E0011.body: From a passage attributed to the metropolitan of Memphis: before the spirit's breath agitated the mass, the parts of the world “lay mingled and inform, brooding overwhelmed in the Abyss of Being” [III.3 ¶46].

E0012.summary: That which is without ground, fathomless or void (Boehme); for Atwood also the Kabalists' name for the Matter, called by them Unknown, Void, Nothing, Infinite.
E0012.body: Quoting Boehme, the text defines it: “the Abysse, that is without ground, or fathomless or void” [III.2 ¶16]; in the same place the One Thing is spoken of as “the first divine manifestation out of the abyss” [III.2 ¶16]. Atwood elsewhere uses the word for the Matter as the Kabalists name it: “that Abyss of the Kabalists, styled also by them Unknown, Void, Nothing, Infinite” [III.2 ¶60], so Abyss = Unknown, Void, Nothing, Infinite.

E0013.summary: A name connected with dissolution, identified by Atwood with the vitriolic solvent; in Hermes and the Master, ‘our Acetum’ with which the soul or sulphurous Form is mingled.
E0013.body: Atwood names it alongside the solvent: something “becomes their vitriolic solvent and most sharp acetum” [I.2 ¶40]; the reader takes it as a name of the dissolving stage, which is an inference. In a passage quoted from Hermes, the watery soul is mingled with it to obtain the sulphurous Form: “to mingle the same with our Acetum” [I.3 ¶27]; the same words recur in a passage quoted from the Master [IV.2 ¶14]. In neither quoted passage is the Acetum itself explained.

E0014.summary: Paired principles that, by action and reaction, raise one another successively until spiritual ability is complete.
E0014.body: Atwood describes the work as “raising successively actives by passives, and, vice versa, passives by actives” [IV.1 ¶41], continuing until spiritual ability is complete. Compare agent and patient.

E0015.summary: Legal measures Atwood cites to illustrate the suppression of transmutation, which only drove its pursuit into secrecy.
E0015.body: Cited by Atwood to illustrate the legal suppression of transmutation, which in her account only drove the pursuit into secrecy [I.1 ¶55; I.1 n61].

E0016.summary: A mystical soil whose glories the prophet describes, spoken of with the winds, clouds, snow and wooden receptacles.
E0016.body: Atwood speaks of “that mystical Adamic Soil” [III.2 ¶12], whose glories the prophet describes, in a context of winds, clouds, snow and wooden receptacles. The text as recorded gives no further plain meaning.

E0017.summary: In the Smaragdine Table of Hermes, the manner by which all things arose from the One Thing.
E0017.body: A term of the Smaragdine Table (Hermes, quoted): “so all things arose from this one thing by adaptation” [I.1 ¶9], and “Hence were all wonderful adaptations of which this is the manner.” [I.1 ¶9]. A second rendering of the Table reads “so all things proceeded from this One Thing by adaptation” [IV.2 ¶44].

E0018.summary: A true master of the Art, one who has accomplished it, sharply distinguished by Atwood from pretenders; in quoted authorities, the initiate whom the Lord illuminates and seals.
E0018.body:
Atwood's usual word for a genuine, accomplished master of the Art. The adepts are those who truly understood Geber: “They who have really understood Geber, his adept compeers” [I.1 ¶33]. They are rare and set against pretenders: “The true adepts have been rare exceptions in the world” [I.1 ¶41]; “Many usurped the title of the adepts, who had no knowledge even of the preliminaries of the Art” [I.1 ¶53]; “the pretenders to the Art were in latter times far more numerous than the true adepts” [I.1 ¶86] (said with reference to Sendivogius). The public could not tell them apart, so “even the true adepts --- for the public knew not to distinguish --- suffered equal cruelty” [I.1 ¶66]. She applies the title to individuals: Ripley “though reputed a good adept” [I.1 ¶64]; “Henry Khunrath, a pious and learned adeptest” [I.1 ¶70].

On their writing: “the adepts appear to have a directly contrary aim” [I.1 ¶82], their writing deliberately obscuring, being “so very abstruse and envious in their disguises” [IV.1 ¶18]; they caution against excitation [IV.1 ¶18]. “Aristotle is much blamed by Adepts in general” [I.1 ¶16], and of the Bononian Enigma “the adepts claim it as having exclusive reference to the occult material of their art” [I.1 ¶20]. A cited speaker says “of a vulgar ignoramus I became a true Adept” [IV.1 ¶17]; Eirenaeus (quoted) says “even one Adept, were he permitted, might impart health to the whole world” [IV.3 ¶26]. “Verily, says the adept” introduces a cited speaker [III.1 ¶8], where the word is also used of those who call the fire of life Antimony.

In quoted patristic passages the adept is the initiate: Clemens Alexandrinus, “he sets his seal upon the adept whom he illuminates with his beams” [II.2 ¶5]; the Bishop of Alexandria, “He sets his seal upon the Adepts” [IV.2 ¶16].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood ties the word to discovery: “The seeker, however, in this point of relation, is the adept, the discoverer, the finder.” [APP ¶23] — the seeker at the point where the Golden Fleece appears.

E0019.summary: The anonymous ‘adept’ or ‘adepts’ whose sayings Atwood cites throughout, almost always in support and sometimes explicitly endorsed, on the matter, the fire, the stages of the work and its spiritual end.
E0019.body:
Atwood frequently quotes an unnamed ‘adept’, sometimes identified only by a footnoted work (*Rosarium*, *Lumen de Lumine*, *Filium Ariadne*, *Introitus Apertus*, *Mercury’s Caducean Rod*, *Maieri Symbola Aureae Mensae*, *Fama et Confessionis, R.C.*), and the adepts collectively. The voice is used in support, and she sometimes endorses it explicitly [III.1 ¶64; III.1 ¶66]. The adept also backs her condemnation of fraudulent books [I.1 ¶53].

**The matter and gold.** “the seed of gold, says the adept, is a fiery form of Light inspissate, and this is the Stone of Fire” [I.2 ¶44; I.2 n43]; “Our gold is not common gold, says the adept, but a depurated substance” [I.3 n63; I.3 n70]. The subject is despised: “It is what the world cares not for, as the adept says, but disesteems it” [II.2 ¶18]. The adepts teach that all things derive from one Spirit, gold nearest it [I.2 ¶48]; purified sulphur as seed and mercury as earth of the wise [I.3 n29; I.3 n30]; the Matter's birth is “singular and not without a miracle” [III.3 ¶62]; “Our golden water, says the adept, is not found in wells” [III.3 ¶17; III.3 n7].

**Fire and process.** “men neither see nor do they believe there is any other fire but the common fire” [I.3 n41]; the three fires “should be quickly lighted” with a Fourth supervening [IV.2 ¶11; IV.2 n2]; “O happy gate of Blackness!” [II.3 ¶37; II.3 n44]; the Seed of Spirit is “a decompounded ens, extremely heavy, shining through the darkness like a fiery star” [II.3 ¶30]; “he that has once passed the Aquaster, and entered the Fire World” [II.3 ¶41] (extent of quotation unclear); “Open the compound creature; look up the elements; divide the elements, and you shall find the quintessential nature” [II.3 ¶52]; on renewal of the powder, “if the process fails in any stage, an addition of the same will renew it” [II.1 ¶25]; Nature alone cannot enter the True Light: “she has no hands” [III.2 ¶61; III.2 n45]; the Orient Animal is stripped “not with arrows or clubs, but with the Hand, as Adepts say” [III.1 ¶64]. Also cited: the sign of returning colours and the white elixir, “now our king hath triumphed over the miseries of death” [I.3 n22]; a reading of ‘dust of the earth’ [I.3 n51]; the Preparing Spirit and cleansing of the Argent vive [IV.1 ¶10]; the guide [II.3 n37]; the Light becoming visible, “Lux manifeste et visibilis ad oculum” [III.3 ¶10], and “the bridegroom crowneth the bride in the North!”, glossed by Atwood as the Light arising out of the crucifixion of cerebral life [III.3 ¶15]; the purified substance's endless transformations [III.2 ¶22; III.2 n22]; the loadstone, Salt, Pole and Fire and the union of agent and patient [IV.2 ¶30; IV.2 n19]; nature's ordinary manifestation contradicting her perfect law [I.2 ¶18; I.2 ¶20]; imaginative impressures lingering in a place [III.4 ¶42].

**Spiritual end.** The Corner Stone is “known, as the Adept says, only to the Wise” [III.1 ¶66]; “Salvation is nothing else but a Transmutation” [IV.2 ¶18; IV.2 n16], which Atwood completes and extends; the adepts' maxim “they who sow in tears shall reap in joy” she expands into the sacrifice of Self-Will [III.3 ¶20]; they say “Natus est jam Elias Artista” [IV.2 ¶12] (our rendering: Elias the Artist is now born) and concealed the three operations [IV.2 ¶3]; with Plutarch they witness to the fable's meaning [IV.2 ¶7]; God “has always revealed them to his elected children” [IV.4 ¶25]. Their analysis of man's life as a pure fire in an ethereal vapour is reported ‘as they profess’ yet presented by Atwood as shown [IV.4 ¶4].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) the Adepts call the Art “Holy Alchemy” [APP ¶29], and reducing their ground to physical science is dismissed as twaddle [APP ¶30].

E0020.summary: A solitary adept of Alexandria, named as the master of Morienus.
E0020.body: Named by Atwood as a solitary adept of Alexandria and Morienus's master [I.1 ¶35].

E0021.summary: Bound up with sacrifice and prayer; its three terms contain all the Divine measures, and its end is where rational inquiry rests and true love is found.
E0021.body: Atwood connects adoration with sacrifice and the advantages of prayer. She speaks of “these three terms of adoration, in which, according to the authorities, all the Divine measures are contained” [III.4 ¶25]; these reconcile the warring elements of life and give three supernal benefits. “And thus the end of all adoration is attained” [III.4 ¶26] — the point at which rational inquiry rests and true love is found.

E0022.summary: In Khunrath, the starting matter of the first act, whose bonds of coagulation are relaxed; called Saturn, the lead of the Wise.
E0022.body: From Khunrath (quoted): the matter of the first act, whose bonds of coagulation are relaxed, called “our heart of Saturn” [IV.1 ¶36]. The text gives its identity: “Adrop (which in its proper tongue is called Saturn, i.e., the lead of the Wise)” [IV.1 ¶36]; so Adrop = Saturn = lead of the Wise.

E0023.summary: The externally generated form imposed on a body, to be constricted, set against the body's inner central form, to be developed into life and act.
E0023.body: Atwood contrasts two forms in a body: “the adventitious or externally generated image may be constricted utterly, and the central form contrariwise developed into life and act” [I.2 ¶20]. The work, on this account, suppresses the outward image and brings forth the inner form.

E0024.summary: The temple's interior sanctuary, entered by the Aspirant after leaving the statues behind; an image of the mind entertaining the simple Unity of Light within.
E0024.body: Atwood uses the image of “the Aspirant entering into the interior to behold the Adytum, leaves behind him all the statues in the temple” [III.2 ¶66], as a figure of the mind entertaining the simple Unity of Light within. She also speaks of approaching “to the gate of the first Adytum” [III.3 ¶3], whose vestibule is where the Tears of Isis are contemplated.

E0025.summary: In Proclus, the soul's innermost recess, where with closed eye she perceives the genus of the gods.
E0025.body: Quoted from Proclus: the soul withdraws “into her interior recesses and into the Adytum of Life” [II.4 ¶29], where with closed eye she perceives the genus of the gods.

E0026.summary: A riddling inscription, unattributed in the text, describing a thing that is none of the opposites yet all, cited after the claim that the Matter is one Identity.
E0026.body: An unattributed riddling inscription cited after Atwood's claim that the Matter is one Identity; it describes something that is none of the opposites yet all, nowhere in particular yet everywhere: “No male, nor female, nor hermaphrodite,” [III.3 ¶66].

E0027.summary: Book 6 of the Aeneid, cited for its descent to the shades, which Atwood reads as an illustration of stages of the work and of the Epopteia of Universal Nature.
E0027.body:
Atwood quotes Book 6 in Latin to illustrate the inner journey. The apparitions: “Corripit hic subita trepidus formidine ferrum” [II.3 ¶21; II.3 n16] (ours: here, trembling with sudden fear, he seizes his sword), as Aeneas draws on bodiless shades until warned. The place of shades: “Umbrarum hic locus est, somni noctisque soporae” [II.3 ¶26; II.3 n28] (ours: this is the place of shades, of sleep and drowsy night). The courage required: “Nunc animis opus, Aenea, nunc pectore firmo.” [II.3 n37] (ours: now, Aeneas, there is need of courage, now of a firm heart). Aeneas meeting his father in Elysium receives the Epopteia of Universal Nature, spirit and mind pervading the whole: “Spiritus intus alit” [II.4 ¶21; II.4 ¶22; II.4 n14] (ours: a spirit within nourishes).

In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), where the author is not named, the drawn sword illustrates the light of reason confronting and dispersing the images in the vital chaos: “Strictamqu Aeneas aciem venientibus offert” [APP ¶165] (ours: Aeneas offers the drawn blade to those coming); Aeneas, the Golden Bough, Tartarus and Elysium are read as stages of the work [APP ¶166; APP ¶168; APP ¶171].

E0028.summary: The incombustible moisture in which, according to the Alchemists, the thick fire of life is imprisoned; unpurified, it is Hades.
E0028.body: A view of the Alchemists that Atwood endorses: the life is “a thick fire imprisoned in a certain incombustible aerial moisture” [II.3 ¶29]. Unpurified, this moisture is Hades [II.3 ¶29].

E0029.summary: Named as Hippocrates' paternal ancestor, honoured with Hercules, a demigod among the Greeks and, for Atwood, modern Mesmerism's only just pride.
E0029.body: Atwood names him as Hippocrates' paternal ancestor, honoured together with Hercules, a demigod only among the Greeks, and the only just pride of modern Mesmerism [IV.3 ¶32; IV.3 ¶34; IV.3 ¶36].

E0030.summary: The imparted spirit whose reception gives wisdom by awakening a consciousness related to the universal.
E0030.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood speaks of “the wisdom imparted by the reception of the Afflatus” [APP ¶41]; its reception awakens a consciousness related to the universal.

E0031.summary: The spirit, which vivifies and holds together the particles of the matter and is superior to the body in operation; paired with the patient.
E0031.body: Atwood calls the spirit “the agent, because it vivifies and holds the particles of the matter together” [I.3 n37], superior to the body in operation. Elsewhere she warns “lest the sin of the agent be multiplied in the patient” [IV.3 ¶56], where the agent is not further defined. See agent and patient.

E0032.summary: The active and receptive parties of the work, which act and react on one another progressively and, after Hermetic dissolution, are one identity.
E0032.body: Atwood: after Hermetic dissolution “the agent and the patient are one identity” [I.2 ¶48]. The work is progressive action and reaction between them: “The whole work is an action of agent on patient, and the reaction of patient, advancing, on agent.” [APP ¶111] (Appendix, Table Talk, later layer). The work may be protracted “by the indisposition of patients, as by the ignorance of agents” [IV.1 ¶17], terms not further defined there. Compare actives / passives.
